# Siṅgāla Sutta (DN 31 (PTS DN iii 180))

**ID:** DN 31 (PTS DN iii 180)  
**Section:** Dīghanikāya (dn)  
**Collection:** Sutta  
**Title (Pali):** Siṅgāla Sutta  
**PTS:** DN iii 180  
**tipitaka.org (CST):** [https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0103m.mul7.xml](https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0103m.mul7.xml)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Siṅgāla Sutta* (DN 31), also known as the *Sigālovāda Sutta* or *Sigālaka Sutta*, is the thirty-first discourse of the *Dīghanikāya* [Bodhi 2005]. Set near Rājagaha at the Bamboo Grove, the discourse takes place when the Buddha meets a young householder named Singālaka (or Sigālaka) who had risen early to worship the six cardinal directions in accordance with his deceased father's wishes [Buddhist Virtues in Socio-Economic Development 2011]. The Buddha reinterprets this ritual into a comprehensive code of moral discipline and social ethics for the laity, often described as "The Layperson's Code of Discipline" [Bodhi 2005]. Rather than performing external rites, the householder is instructed to honor reciprocal relationships across six social dimensions, including the fivefold mutual duties binding parents and children, teachers and pupils, and husbands and wives [Young 2004; Bodhi 2005]. The text combines prose instruction with stanzas introduced by traditional speech tags [Winternitz 1933; Anandajoti 2010].
